correctness.rationale: The proof was reconstructed directly from graph distances. For an edge \(e_{ij}=a_i b_j\), \(a_k\) reports 0 at the tail index, 2 at the missing matched head index, and 1 otherwise, with the symmetric rule for \(b_k\). If two matched pairs are absent, two edges using a third index have identical codes, so at least \(n-1\) matched pairs must be represented. Conversely, choosing one vertex from every matched pair except one makes every represented index distinguish tail, head, and neither, which uniquely identifies every edge. Minimum size then forces exactly one chosen vertex in each represented pair and gives \(n2^{n-1}\) bases. Independent exhaustive enumeration for \(3\le n\le7\) matched the theorem exactly.

evidence: Later work on the maximum edge metric dimension concerns \(\operatorname{edim}(G)=|V(G)|-1\), while the crown value here is \(n-1\) on \(2n\) vertices.
The connected-bipartite \(n-2\) characterization likewise does not cover the claimed value.

value.rationale: Crown graphs are a canonical symmetric family and a minimal structured deletion of \(K_{n,n}\). The theorem gives the exact parameter, classifies every optimizer, and exhibits a substantial sensitivity phenomenon: deleting one perfect matching changes the edge metric dimension from \(2n-2\) to \(n-1\). This is a natural family theorem, not an arbitrary finite slice.
residual_risks: The result is restricted to connected crowns \(n\ge3\) and ordinary edge metric dimension.
